title: Reported phishing email
symptoms: A person reports a suspicious email, a fake invoice, or a vendor payment message. The message may contain a link or an attachment. They may have almost clicked it. Nothing on the workstation has executed yet.
steps:
1. Tell the reporter not to click links, open attachments, or reply.
2. Preserve the original message. Collect the full headers, the sender address, the reply-to address, the subject, and the URL or the attachment hash.
3. Search mail for the same sender, reply-to, subject, or URL. Count how many mailboxes received it.
4. Block the sender domain and the URL at the mail gateway. Quarantine matching messages that are still unread.
5. Reset the reporter's password and revoke their sessions only if they clicked the link, opened the attachment, or entered credentials. Otherwise leave the account alone.
6. If they entered credentials, stop and look up the compromised-account runbook before doing anything else.

title: Ransomware file encryption
symptoms: Files on a host were renamed with a new extension, documents no longer open, or a ransom note on the desktop demands bitcoin or another cryptocurrency. An encrypting process may still be running.
steps:
1. Isolate the host from the network. Do not power it off. Do not reboot it.
2. Record the encrypting process name, pid, and command line if it is still running. Do not kill it until that is captured.
3. Copy the ransom note. Record the new file extension and one encrypted file path.
4. Do not restore files onto the same volume. Do not delete Volume Shadow Copies. Do not pay the ransom.
5. Identify the earliest host and the earliest timestamp with the same extension or the same note. That host is the first scope of the incident.
6. Tell the incident lead the host name, the extension, and whether the process is still running.

title: Compromised user account
symptoms: The same account signed in from two countries an hour apart, a password showed up in a leak, or the user approved a flood of MFA push prompts they did not start. A session is already open.
steps:
1. Disable the account. Do not delete it.
2. Revoke active sessions, refresh tokens, and application passwords.
3. Remove any MFA device, inbox rule, or OAuth grant added in the last 7 days that the user does not recognize.
4. Reset the password only after the sessions are revoked. Require the user to register MFA again.
5. List the secrets, mailboxes, and source repositories the account could read. Rotate those secrets.
6. Record the sign-in time, source IP, and user agent of the suspicious session for the handoff.

title: Internet-facing service on a vulnerable version
symptoms: A public service, VPN portal, or remote access gateway is running a product version named in a critical vendor advisory. A scanner or Shodan may have shown the exposure. Exploitation is not yet confirmed.
steps:
1. Confirm the product name and the exact version, and confirm the service is reachable from the internet.
2. If a patch is not ready in this maintenance window, block the vulnerable port or URL path at the edge. Restarting the process is not a fix.
3. List every asset running that version, not only the one that was reported.
4. On those assets, look for exploitation: a new admin user, a webshell, or an unexpected child process of the vulnerable service.
5. Apply the vendor patch and confirm the version string changed.
6. Keep the edge block in place until the version check passes.

title: Suspicious living-off-the-land execution
symptoms: A user document or a browser download started a living-off-the-land binary. Typical cases are Excel or Word launching encoded PowerShell, or a browser download launching mshta, rundll32, or regsvr32. The host has not been reimaged.
steps:
1. Isolate the workstation. Do not reimage it yet.
2. Capture the full process tree, the command line, and the parent process before you kill anything. Parents that matter are Office, the browser, and explorer.
3. Treat encoded PowerShell, rundll32, mshta, or regsvr32 started from a document or a browser download as malicious.
4. Hash the dropped file or the document that was opened. Search other hosts for that hash.
5. Check for persistence created in the same hour: a scheduled task, a Run key, a new service, or a startup-folder item.
6. Do not wipe the disk. Hand the host name, the parent process, and the hash to the incident lead.
